item.title: Cycling Naoshima Art Island — Guide
item.description: Naoshima is small enough to explore by bicycle, and renting one is one of the best ways to experience the art island. With a bike — standard or electric-assist, useful for the island’s hills — you can move freely between the Benesse Art Site museums, the Art House Project in the old village, Kusama’s yellow and red pumpkins, quiet beaches and coastal viewpoints, all at your own pace and without waiting for buses.

item.title: Naoshima Art Island: A Day Trip from Okayama — Guide
item.description: Naoshima is a small island in the Seto Inland Sea that has become one of the most celebrated contemporary art destinations on earth. From the 1990s, the Benesse corporation and architect Tadao Ando remade it: concrete museums are sunk into the hillsides so as not to intrude on the landscape, works by Monet, Turrell and De Maria sit in purpose-built chambers, Yayoi Kusama’s spotted pumpkins stand on the piers, and in the village of Honmura old wooden houses have been converted into individual artworks.

item.title: Naoshima: Japan's Art Island — Guide
item.description: Naoshima is one of the world’s great art destinations, a small island in the Seto Inland Sea reborn as an open-air museum of contemporary art and architecture. At its heart is the Benesse Art Site, a series of museums and installations, several designed by architect Tadao Ando, that merge art, buildings and the seascape. The Chichu Art Museum, built largely underground to preserve the island’s profile, shows works by Monet, James Turrell and Walter De Maria in spaces sculpted around natural light.
